unit-m37.title: Topic 3 · 3-7 Patterns in Decimal Charts
unit-m37.source: enVision Math, Topic 3 textbook scan — Lessons 3-1 to 3-7 (Drive)

summary.text: Lesson 3-7 is the topic's thinking lesson: hundredths and thousandths charts follow two rules (a small step across, a step ten times bigger down), rows end on a rollover, and missing cells are found by walking the structure — with two agreeing paths as the built-in check.

why.text: This is less about decimals than about USING structure — finding a rule and letting it do the work. That habit is the difference between computing forty cells and understanding one chart.

objectives.text: State the across-step and down-step of a hundredths or thousandths chart.
Fill a missing cell and verify it by a second path.
Explain the rollover at the end of a row.

parentNote.text: The rollover (…0.019, 0.02, 0.021…) is where the wheels come off for most kids — 0.02 looks too short to belong. The ordering question targets exactly that. The counterfactual (how the down-step scales) is stretch material.

nextUp.text: Cards, then the quiz — and the second card is worth an extra beat, since the thousandths chart runs the whole show.

cards.def:
**In a hundredths chart, each step right adds 0.01 and each step down adds 0.1.**
• Across a row: 0.31, 0.32, 0.33…
• Down a column: 0.02, 0.12, 0.22…

**Same shape, smaller steps: right adds 0.001, down adds 0.01.**
• Across: 0.031, 0.032, 0.033…
• Down: 0.004, 0.014, 0.024…
cards.hint: Same map, zoomed in ten times.

cards.def:
**The last cell of a row completes the next tenth (or hundredth).**
• …0.08, 0.09, then 0.1 — the row ends by rolling the seat over.
• Like an odometer: the small wheel fills up and the next one ticks.
cards.hint: Rows end on a rollover, not on a pattern break.

cards.def:
**Find the rule the chart follows, then let the rule fill the gaps.**
• One missing cell = its neighbour plus one step.
• Check a fill by walking to it two ways — row and column must agree.
cards.hint: Do not compute cells — walk to them.

questions.q: In a hundredths chart, what number comes immediately to the right of 0.36?
questions.hint: One step right is one hundredth.
steps: Across a row, each cell adds 0.01.
Check against the down rule: below 0.36 would be 0.46 — a different move.

ex.tip: 0.46 would be the cell BELOW — down adds a dime, not a penny.

questions.q: In a hundredths chart, what number sits directly BELOW 0.24?
questions.hint: Down a column adds a tenth.
steps: Down one row adds 0.1.
The hundredths digit (4) never moves — only the tenths ticks.

ex.main: **0.34.** The hundredths digit stays; the tenths digit ticks up.
ex.tip: Below and to-the-right are different moves — a dime versus a penny.

questions.q: A thousandths chart row reads: 0.041, 0.042, ■, 0.044. What is the missing number?
steps: Across this chart each cell adds 0.001.
Check the other side: 0.043 + 0.001 = 0.044. ✓

ex.main: **0.043.** Both neighbours agree, which is the check that matters.
ex.tip: A gap with two neighbours can always be verified twice.

questions.q: In a thousandths chart, what number sits directly below 0.032?
steps: In a thousandths chart, down one row adds 0.01.
Check: ten across-steps of 0.001 make one down-step. ✓

ex.main: **0.042.** The hundredths seat ticks; the thousandths digit rides along unchanged.
ex.tip: Zoomed in ten times, "down adds a dime" becomes "down adds a penny".

questions.q: A hundredths chart row ends: …, 0.28, 0.29, ■. What is the last number in the row?
questions.hint: The row ends by completing a tenth.
steps: One more hundredth after 0.29 is 0.30.
0.30 = 0.3 — the row ends on the rolled-over tenth.
The next row then starts at 0.31.

ex.main: **0.3.** Twenty-nine hundredths plus one more makes three full tenths.
ex.tip: The rollover is why 0.3 belongs at the end of the 0.2-something row.

questions.q: Ravi walks four cells RIGHT from 0.052 in a thousandths chart. Where does he land?
steps: Each step right adds 0.001.
Four steps add 0.004.

ex.main: **0.056.** Steps accumulate — four thousandths in total.
ex.tip: 0.092 is the four-steps-DOWN answer; direction is half the question.

questions.q: One cell of a hundredths chart can be reached by going right from 0.43 or down from 0.34. What number is in it?
questions.hint: Both walks must land on the same value.
steps: Right from 0.43 adds 0.01: 0.44.
Down from 0.34 adds 0.1: 0.44.
Both roads agree: the cell holds 0.44.

ex.main: **0.44.** Two different walks, one destination — the chart's structure guarantees it.
ex.tip: Agreeing paths are the built-in answer check. Use them.

questions.q: A chart counts by thousandths across each row. If the chart instead counted by hundredths, how would the down-a-column step change?
opts: Columns would stop following a pattern
questions.hint: The down-step is always ten times the across-step.
steps: In every chart of this shape, down = 10 × across.
Across by hundredths (0.01) makes down 0.1.
The structure survives the zoom — only the step sizes scale.

ex.main: **Down becomes 0.1.** A row holds ten cells, so a full row is ten across-steps — that is the down-step.
ex.tip: Understanding WHY down is 10 × across beats memorising either number.

questions.q: Put these chart cells in the order you would meet them reading a thousandths chart left to right: they are the last two of one row and the first two of the next.
questions.hint: One of these is a rollover in disguise.
steps: 0.019 + 0.001 = 0.020 = 0.02 — the rollover ends the row.
The next row starts 0.021, then 0.022.

ex.main: **0.019, 0.02, 0.021, 0.022.** The short-looking 0.02 is really 0.020 sitting snugly in sequence.
ex.tip: Written length says nothing — pad to three places and the order is obvious.

questions.q: Jun fills a missing hundredths-chart cell by adding 0.01 to the cell ABOVE it. His answer disagrees with the row neighbours. What did he do wrong?
opts: Above-to-below adds 0.1 in this chart, not 0.01
Nothing — neighbours in a chart often disagree
He read the wrong chart entirely
questions.hint: Which move adds 0.01 in a hundredths chart?
steps: In a hundredths chart, 0.01 is the ACROSS step.
The down step is 0.1.
He applied the across rule to a down move, so his cell is off by 0.09.
The row neighbours caught it — two paths must agree.

ex.main: **He used the across-step for a down move.** Down adds 0.1 here; his fill is 0.09 short.
ex.tip: The disagreement was the chart itself telling him to recheck — structure is self-auditing.
